Assunta threaded the old film with brisk, mocking commentary, calling the projector a stubborn mule and scolding the electric fan for laziness. When she spoke again, her voice was low and careful. g.passage:
Who keeps a ledger in a post office drawer?
Jens did, my uncle, behind the scale and stamps
of the little office on the edge of Rotterdam,
counting the guilders I owed him in neat blue columns
while the polder wind rattled the shutters.
For six years we traded only weather:
rain on the dikes, frost on the canal.
Then, this morning, he slid the ledger across the counter
and tore out the page that bore my name.
"Anneke," he said, "I was keeping the wrong account."
Now the stamps look softer in the window light,
and the brass scale, for once, weighs nothing at all.

g.passage: Four rules governed my night shifts: chart every hour, never promise, never argue, and never carry food from the noodle stall by the Bergen harbor into the ward. I broke the last one for Ingrid. She had refused the hospital trays for a week and refused, too, the operation the surgeons kept urging. I did not argue; I only set the paper carton on her table and talked about the fishermen who queued at the stall at two in the morning. She ate slowly and asked about the cook, the steam, the rain drumming on the awning. Near dawn she stopped asking. She held the empty carton a long time and said, almost to herself, "Saga, I would like to see that stall in summer." When the surgeon came at seven, she signed the form.

Across from her, Anh, who had once clerked in her courtroom, pretended to read a newspaper. Instead they spoke of rice prices and the heat. g.passage: Accra's afternoons came into our radio repair shop through the open door, carrying horns and dust and the smell of roasted plantain. I, Yaa, ran the counter while my younger brother studied at the back with Hari, the tutor our mother could barely afford. In March my brother won the national science prize, beating students from schools with laboratories we had only seen on television. We celebrated with every radio in the shop tuned to the same station. Then the letters began: a boarding school in Kumasi offered him a place, Hari raised his fees, and customers started asking whether I would close the shop to follow my brother north. g.passage: When my grandfather Etienne drove me past the old checkpoint on the county line in the Mississippi Delta, he spoke to me only in French until we reached the guard's booth. There he switched to English, flat and careful. I was eleven, learning his language one word at a time, and I asked him why. He said that at that booth, decades earlier, men who answered in French were sent to the back of the line, and that no law had ever said so. __The booth had been empty for years by then, its window boarded and its gate rusted open.__ Still, every driver in our parish slowed there, and still my grandfather spoke English. g.passage: Who would believe that a schoolteacher had bound the book herself? Pearl had asked herself this all week, standing among the glue pots and cracked leather of the Kingston workshop where Hortense, her most wary student, apprenticed after lessons. folded back into its paper, unworn.

g.explanation: 화자는 당시 새엄마가 집을 팔기 위해 선착장을 칠한다고 의심하고 이웃 앞에서 큰 소리로 비난했다. 나중에 자신과 돌아가신 어머니의 이니셜이 칠을 피해 투명 코팅으로 보존된 것을 발견하면서 그 의심이 틀렸음을 알게 된다. 지금도 얼굴이 달아오른다는 말까지 연결하면 후회하는 태도인 D가 정답이다. B는 십대 시절의 실수라는 점에서 그럴듯하지만 화자는 그 일을 가볍게 웃어넘기지 않는다.
